items: Running git fetch and expecting it to heal the repository. Root cause: a fetch negotiates by commits, and the refs say every commit is present, so nothing is requested.
Unpacking a good copy over the damaged file. Root cause: git unpack-objects does not write an object that already exists in the repository, and the damaged file has that name.
Deleting the clone as the first step. Root cause: the clone may hold commits, stashes and reflogs that exist nowhere else; a fresh clone has only what the server has.
Treating dangling lines as corruption. Root cause: dangling means unreachable and unreferenced; only missing, broken and error lines describe damage.
Keeping a repository in a file-syncing folder. Root cause: such tools copy files one by one without Git's locking, which the Git FAQ names as a cause of missing objects and broken refs.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. An ML engineer keeps a training repository inside a cloud-synced folder so that a notebook server and a laptop "share" it.
The lead's procedure follows the chapter.
One more commit existed only locally.
The statement to the CTO is exact: what was damaged, what repaired it, what existed only on that machine, and what was changed so that it doesn't happen again.
Your turn. Do Exercise 12.8, Level 3, "The backup that will not clone", in exercises/m11-m15-investigation-recovery.md.
Before you run anything, predict which commands will still succeed on the damaged repository and which will fail, and say which objects each has to read.
The challenge is Exercise 12.12, Level 5, "Power loss in the middle of a commit", in the same file.

slides.direction: Q196: "`git fsck` reports `missing tree`. Why does `git fetch` not repair it, and what does?"
slides.label: Q196
quotes: git fsck reports missing tree. Why does git fetch not repair it, and what does?

slides.lead: Let's land this. You should now be able to say:
items: Damage is an object that a ref still reaches and that cannot be read; git fsck calls it missing or broken, never dangling.
A fetch does not repair it, because the negotiation is by commits and my refs say I have them all.
The same object from any repository is the same bytes; I can unpack it from a healthy clone after moving the damaged file aside, or refetch everything.
A corrupt index is rebuilt with git reset; only the record of what was staged is lost.
I can list what Git cannot recover, and for each item say that no object was written or that the object and its names are gone.

slides.body: Read sections 13.11 and 13.12 of Chapter 13. Then write the CTO statement that Q199 of the question bank asks for.
Today you diagnosed real damage and repaired it two ways.

beats.text: A repository has worked for weeks. git status is clean. git log --oneline prints the history. Then one day somebody runs git log --stat, and Git stops with an error about a data stream and a corrupt object.
beats.tele: A repository has worked for weeks. `git status` is clean. `git log --oneline` prints the history. Then one day somebody runs `git log --stat`, and Git stops with an error about a data stream and a corrupt object.

beats.text: The engineer's first move is the one almost everyone makes: git fetch, which downloads the objects the server has and you lack. It exits with status 0 and prints nothing. The error is still there. The second move is to delete the clone and start over. Fine if everything was pushed, and a loss if it wasn't.
beats.tele: The engineer's first move is the one almost everyone makes: `git fetch`, which downloads the objects the server has and you lack. It exits with status 0 and prints nothing. The error is still there. The second move is to delete the clone and start over. Fine if everything was pushed, and a loss if it wasn't.

beats.text: Your CTO's question is short: "Is the repository damaged, how badly, and can you fix it without losing what is only on that machine?" To answer, you need to know why a fetch doesn't help, and what does. Remember that silent fetch.
beats.tele: Your CTO's question is short: "Is the repository damaged, how badly, and can you fix it without losing what is only on that machine?" To answer, you need to know why a fetch doesn't help, and what does. Remember that silent fetch.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Every recovery so far was about a lost name. The object existed, and you had to find it and point a ref at it. An object is one stored unit, named by a hash of its content. A ref is a name that holds an object ID.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Every recovery so far was about a lost name. The object existed, and you had to find it and point a ref at it. An object is one stored unit, named by a hash of its content. A ref is a name that holds an object ID.

beats.text: Today is the other kind of problem: an object that's still needed can't be read. A reachable commit, tree or blob, one that a ref still leads to, is missing or corrupt.
beats.tele: Today is the other kind of problem: an object that's still needed can't be read. A reachable commit, tree or blob, one that a ref still leads to, is missing or corrupt.

beats.text: The causes are outside Git: failing hardware, and tools that copy the repository file by file. The Git FAQ is direct about the second. It says not to use a cloud syncing service to sync any portion of a Git repository, "since this can cause corruption, such as missing objects, changed or added files, broken refs".

It says not to use a cloud syncing service to sync any portion of a Git repository, "since this can cause corruption, such as missing objects, changed or added files, broken refs".

beats.text: The symptom. Commands that need the object fail. Commands that don't need it keep working, which is why damage can go unnoticed for weeks. git status and git log --oneline read commits and the index, your proposed next commit. git log --stat needs trees and blobs: directory listings and file contents.
beats.tele: The symptom. Commands that need the object fail. Commands that don't need it keep working, which is why damage can go unnoticed for weeks. `git status` and `git log --oneline` read commits and the index, your proposed next commit. `git log --stat` needs trees and blobs: directory listings and file contents.

beats.text: The diagnosis. git fsck verifies that everything reachable is present and well formed, and its words for damage differ from the harmless reports of the earlier videos. dangling is information. Lines that begin with missing, broken or error describe a repository that needs repair. A file that's present but unreadable counts as missing.
beats.tele: The diagnosis. `git fsck` verifies that everything reachable is present and well formed, and its words for damage differ from the harmless reports of the earlier videos. `dangling` is information. Lines that begin with `missing`, `broken` or `error` describe a repository that needs repair. A file that's present but unreadable counts as missing.

beats.text: Why a fetch does not repair it. A fetch negotiates by commits. Your repository says which commits it has, and the server sends what isn't reachable from them. Now the names: main and origin/main, your record of the server's branch, sit on the same commit. Your refs say you have everything. So the server sends nothing.
beats.tele: Why a fetch does not repair it. A fetch negotiates by commits. Your repository says which commits it has, and the server sends what isn't reachable from them. Now the names: `main` and `origin/main`, your record of the server's branch, sit on the same commit. Your refs say you have everything. So the server sends nothing.

beats.text: What does repair it. An object's ID is determined by its content. So the same object from any other repository is the object you lost. There are two routes.
beats.tele: What does repair it. An object's ID is determined by its content. So the same object from any other repository is the object you lost. There are two routes.

beats.text: The precise route: ask a healthy clone for a pack that contains the object, and unpack it in the damaged repository. git pack-objects reads IDs on standard input and writes a pack, one file that stores many objects. git unpack-objects stores the objects of a pack as loose files.
beats.tele: The precise route: ask a healthy clone for a pack that contains the object, and unpack it in the damaged repository. `git pack-objects` reads IDs on standard input and writes a pack, one file that stores many objects. `git unpack-objects` stores the objects of a pack as loose files.

beats.text: One detail decides whether it works. git unpack-objects doesn't write objects that already exist in the repository, and a damaged file with that name exists. Move it out first. Move it, don't delete it: the official how-to on this subject asks you to keep it, since a corrupt object can only be analysed next to its intact twin.
beats.tele: One detail decides whether it works. `git unpack-objects` doesn't write objects that already exist in the repository, and a damaged file with that name exists. Move it out first. Move it, don't delete it: the official how-to on this subject asks you to keep it, since a corrupt object can only be analysed next to its intact twin.

beats.text: The blunt route: git fetch --refetch, which in the manual's words "fetches all objects as a fresh clone would". The release notes of Git 2.36, which added it, describe it as useful "when you cannot trust what you have in the local object store".
beats.tele: The blunt route: `git fetch --refetch`, which in the manual's words "fetches all objects as a fresh clone would". The release notes of Git 2.36, which added it, describe it as useful "when you cannot trust what you have in the local object store".

beats.text: The limit. --refetch can only bring back what the server has. Commits that exist only in your clone and lost an object are repaired from your own working tree, the files you edit, if the file is still there, with git hash-object -w. Otherwise they're lost from that point of history on.
beats.tele: The limit. `--refetch` can only bring back what the server has. Commits that exist only in your clone and lost an object are repaired from your own working tree, the files you edit, if the file is still there, with `git hash-object -w`. Otherwise they're lost from that point of history on.

says: --refetch can only bring back what the server has

beats.text: A corrupt index is the mild case. Every command that looks at the working tree fails with "bad signature" and "index file corrupt". History commands still work. The index is derived data, except for one thing: the record of what you had staged. Move the file away, and git reset builds a new index from HEAD without touching the working tree. Your edits are still in the files. What's gone is the distinction between staged and unstaged.
